_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 2 Bugs and Predictions. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (output; a bug; correcting it, with the edit part appended in 2026-09-16; precise, not vague; linear algorithms). Both of the lesson's own prediction algorithms are predicted and then checked, which is what 2CT.05 asks for. Every wrong ORDER is drawn by handing the lesson's own scene the wrong list - ART.scene(tea, [water]) paints the puddle and writes its own caption - and every wrong STEP is marked on the step row that is wrong, never on a person.
title: Bugs and Predictions
subtitle: Grade 2 Computing
objectives: Identify and correct a single error in algorithms that represent everyday events or tasks.
Know that an algorithm is a precise set of instructions.

beats.say: Two apples. Take three more. Give one to Sami. What do you end up with?
You can work that out before you do it. And when a step is wrong, you can fix it.

at.work: work that out before you do it

scenes.heading: What you get at the end

beats.say: The output of an algorithm is what you have when every step is done.
Here is the algorithm. Take two apples. Take three more. Give one to Sami.
Say the output before you follow the steps. That is predicting.
Now follow every step with your finger. Two apples.
Take three more, and you have five. Give one away, and you have four.
The output is four apples. If you predicted four, you were right.
Try another. Start with five counters, take two away, add four.
Five, three, seven. The output is seven counters.
A bug is a step that is wrong, or a right step in the wrong place.
Here is a tea algorithm. Cup. A sock in the cup. Hot water. Milk.
A sock in the cup does not belong in a tea algorithm. That step is the bug.
Here is another one. The water is poured before the cup is there.
Pouring the water is right. Doing it too early is the bug.
Finding the bug is half the job. Correcting it is the other half.
Do not throw the algorithm away. The rest of it already works. Edit it.
To edit means to change what is already there, and keep the rest.
Swap the sock for a tea bag. Everything else stays as it was.

at.swap: Swap the sock for a tea bag

beats.say: Or move the early step to where it belongs. The cup comes first.
Then run the algorithm again and check. A proper cup of tea.
An algorithm is a precise set of instructions. It leaves nothing to guess.
Turn left at the shop is precise. You know which way and where.
Go somewhere is vague. Vague means you are left guessing. Where?
Take three steps forward is precise. Walk a bit is vague.
A vague instruction makes Robo guess. And Robo guesses badly.
A linear algorithm is a straight line of steps, one after another.
Open the tin. Food in the bowl. Bowl on the floor. Call the cat.
Each step does a job, and each one has its place in the line.
You cannot spoon food out of a tin that is still closed.
Follow it exactly, in a straight line, and the cat is fed.
You can predict the output of an algorithm before you follow it.
A bug is a wrong step, or a right step too early. Find it, then edit it.
A precise instruction leaves nothing to guess, so Robo can follow it.
